summary: This standards-track applicability statement gives guidance on which protocols from the RPL protocol suite to choose and how to use them for home automation and building control. It describes how to meet the needs of those environments, such as many small battery-powered devices on a lossy wireless network.

eli5.summary: This is like a shopping list that says which tools from a big toolbox work best for making lights and thermostats in a house talk to each other.

subtitle: Which parts of the RPL routing suite to use, and with what settings, for lights, thermostats and sensors in homes and buildings.

tldr.problem: RPL was designed for low-power and lossy networks in general. Home and building control adds strict needs: lights must react quickly, links are unreliable, many devices have very little memory, and the network may have no border router at all.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement picks a profile. Use P2P-RPL for reactive point-to-point routes in non-storing mode with Objective Function Zero, use MPL for multicast, secure all RPL messages with a shared key, and use the recommended Trickle and MPL parameter values.
tldr.outcome: It gives implementers concrete choices and ranges for home automation and building control. The RFC itself warns that following it does not guarantee full interoperability.

facts.label: Response time target
facts.value: 250 ms (soft real-time); 200 ms deadline for MPL

today: RFC 7733 is a Proposed Standard from February 2016, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the applicability statement for RPL in home and building control, and it stresses that its guidance alone does not ensure interoperability.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This applicability statement guides the use of the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) protocol suite in two domains: home automation and building automation. It is based on the requirements documents RFC 5826 (home) and RFC 5867 (building). The Advanced Metering Infrastructure is also considered where appropriate.

The two domains share two key properties. The network may be cut off from the ISP and must still give occupants control, so routing has to work without a border router. And links are unreliable while reactions must be instant and very reliable. The differences are mostly in commissioning, maintenance and the user interface, so this document concentrates on reliability, timeliness and local routing.

It builds on core RPL (RFC 6550) and on RFC 6997, which adds reactive point-to-point route discovery, and it complements the threat analysis in RFC 7416. The network diameter considered is at most 10 hops, typically five. Urban and industrial networks, which can be much larger, are out of scope.

The RFC cautions that adherence to its guidance does not necessarily give fully interoperable solutions, and that additional rigorous, managed programs will be needed for that.
sections.eli5: Houses and office buildings need their light switches and sensors to work quickly even if the internet is down. This paper says which parts of a big networking toolbox to use for that job.

sections.title: The Deployment Scenario
sections.content:
A typical home automation network has fewer than 100 nodes. Large buildings may span 10,000 nodes, but they are usually organized into subnetworks of tens to hundreds of nodes, which for critical operations may work independently. The main job is control of light and heating or cooling, using wall controllers plus movement, light and temperature sensors.

The wireless subnetwork can take one of three shapes: a stand-alone network of 10 to 100 nodes with no border router, a connected network with one border router, or a connected network with multiple border routers. Many nodes are battery powered and sleep. Most are Class 0 devices (RFC 7228), such as wall switches, and only a few are Class 1 devices with more memory.

People expect an immediate response. Alarm and light control are treated as soft real-time systems where perceived quality degrades significantly when response times exceed 250 ms. If a light does not react, users press the control again and create bursts of redundant commands.

The RFC recommends keeping the home entertainment network mostly separate from the control network, since it needs high bandwidth that control does not.
sections.eli5: A house has a few dozen gadgets and a big building can have thousands. Many run on batteries and nap a lot, and everyone expects the light to turn on right when they flip the switch.

sections.title: Traffic Patterns and Which Protocol Fits
sections.content:
Most traffic is light point-to-point control, such as Put-Ack or Get-Response. Bulk transfer is used for firmware updates and logs. Group communication is used for service discovery and for groups of lights. Sensors and the equipment they control are usually in the same room, so most senders and receivers are one hop apart. Interference and multipath fading can still cut that one-hop path for a while, so alternative n-hop routes are essential.

The RFC describes five communication paradigms:

  • Source-Sink (SS): many sources to one sink, often via the border router. Use RPL in non-storing mode, with source routing from the border router.
  • Publish-Subscribe (PS): devices register interest in a server's data. It is closely related to SS in building networks.
  • Peer-to-Peer (P2P): device to device in the same subnetwork, often from remote controls or wall controllers, with a stringent low-latency requirement.
  • Peer-to-Multipeer (P2MP): one device sends to several destinations, as when a thermostat tells several fans and valves.
  • Duocast and N-Cast: one transfer to many destinations, such as a presence sensor messaging a set of lights. MPL is preferred.

P2P-RPL is required for all P2P and P2MP traffic inside a wireless subnetwork, excluding the border router. It lets a node wake up and find routes within a few seconds, keeps memory-limited nodes holding only relevant routes, and has a Stop bit so that a target can tell nodes to stop forwarding DIO messages for the temporary DAG, which limits broadcast storms compared with AODV.
sections.eli5: Mostly, a switch talks to a lamp in the same room. So the best plan is a quick shortcut between neighbors, not a long trip through the boss's office and back.

sections.title: The RPL Profile
sections.content:
The core recommendation is that P2P-RPL (RFC 6997) SHOULD be used, because its reactive discovery allows low response times even when routes need repairing on the fly. It also keeps data from passing through the region near the root and shortens paths. For more reliability it can keep two independent P2P source routes per destination, using them alternately. A failed path can be discarded after a timeout, typically 15 minutes.

The profile's main choices:

  • Mode: non-storing mode MUST be used, because many nodes such as light switches have extremely little memory.
  • RPL instances: a node MUST be able to join at least one instance, since each P2P-RPL route discovery creates a temporary instance.
  • DAO: DAO messages are not acknowledged in networks of battery-operated devices, to save power.
  • Metric: Expected Transmission Count (ETX) is RECOMMENDED.
  • Objective Function: Objective Function Zero (OF0) MUST be used, though others MAY be used when circumstances dictate.
  • Repair: P2P-RPL needs no DODAG repair. For SS traffic, local repair (poisoning) is sufficient.
  • Addresses: assigned IPv6 addresses MUST be routable and unique within the routing domain.
  • Layer 2: the profile applies to IEEE 802.15.4 and G.9959 with their IPv6 adaptation layers. Link-layer unicast acknowledgements SHOULD be enabled.

Sleeping nodes and missing border routers matter too. In a constrained deployment a link-layer node such as the coordinator SHOULD act as an authoritative root, sending unicast Router Advertisements with a Unique Local Address prefix during joining, so that a border router can be added later.
sections.eli5: The recipe says: let neighbors quickly find a path when they need one, keep each gadget's notes very short, and have a backup path ready in case the first one breaks.

sections.title: Trickle, P2P-RPL and MPL Parameters
sections.content:
For the RPL control messages, the recommended Trickle values are DIOIntervalMin 4 (which translates to 16 ms), DIOIntervalDoublings 14 and DIORedundancyConstant 1. DIO changes are expected to propagate within 1 to 3 seconds. When nothing happens, the DIO interval grows to 4.37 minutes, and a node hearing no DIO for more than 10 minutes can conclude the connection is lost. The recommended P2P-RPL values are MinHopRankIncrease 1, MaxRankIncrease 0, MaxRank 6 and OF0.

For multicast, MPL (RFC 7731) is the RECOMMENDED protocol. It uses Trickle: a forwarder rebroadcasts a packet at a random time in each interval only if it has heard fewer than k copies. The profile targets a 200 ms deadline for a human action such as switching on lights, over 1 to 10 hops. To raise the chance of meeting it, use a small Imin, fewer MPL intervals and fewer forwarders. The suggested values are:

  • Imin = 10 to 50 ms
  • Imax = 100 to 400 ms
  • k = 2 or 3, with k greater than q, where q = Imin / 3 assuming a 3 ms transmission interval
  • max_expiration = 2 to 4

The RFC also suggests setting the number of MAC buffers and back-off repetitions to 1 and adding a real-time layer between MPL and MAC that drops the oldest messages. It advises configuring the network so that at least two forwarders per hop repeat messages to the same destinations.
sections.eli5: Gadgets shout "anything new?" often at first and then less and less when all is quiet. For group messages, a few neighbors repeat the news fast so every lamp hears it almost at once.

sections.title: Securing RPL and Joining the Network
sections.content:
All RPL messages MUST be secured by RPL message security, link-layer security, or both. RPL MAY use unsecured messages to save size, but if even one node does, link-layer security MUST be used on all nodes. The key is symmetric and MUST be distributed or established securely. The same key MUST NOT be used for both RPL message security and link-layer security between two peers.

The scope of key distribution MUST be no greater than the network, that is, a group key. It MAY be narrower, such as a pairwise key or a subset group key. The mechanism from Section 6.9 of the ZigBee IP specification SHALL be used to distribute a network-wide key. An Authentication Server authenticates the joining node and sends it the network security material over PANA. The authentication stack, top to bottom, is TLS (with a pre-shared key or an elliptic-curve cipher suite), EAP-TLS, EAP, and PANA with a PANA relay (RFC 6345) to cover nodes that are not in radio range of the server. The joining node acts as PANA Client and uses a link-local address based on its EUI-64 for the first exchanges.

If RPL message security is used, the RFC says to SHOULD use: Counter is Time flag 0, Algorithm 0 (CCM with AES-128), Key Identifier Mode 10 (group key with Key Source and Key Index) and Security Level 0 (MAC-32). Integrity is the basic need, and encryption is unlikely to be necessary given the largely non-confidential RPL payloads.
sections.eli5: A new gadget must show it is allowed in, like a guest showing a pass at the door. After that it gets the club's secret handshake, and all messages use it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security considerations of RFC 6997, RFC 6550 and RFC 7731, plus the attacks and countermeasures in RFC 7416. A shared key must be distributed securely, a network identity configured, and the key stored so it is hard for unauthorized parties to read. A Layer 2 mechanism is mandated for initial and incremental deployment.

At initial deployment the network is secured by securing nodes one after another at the link layer. In homes, a simple procedure such as pressing buttons at the same time on a secured device and an unsecured joining device may be enough. In buildings an installer uses a tool that sets up a secure path to the joining node. New nodes later join through an assisting node. If a node is found compromised, all trusted nodes that share keys with it need to be rekeyed.

No multicast security solution is specified. Networks depend on Layer 2 security to keep outsiders from sending multicast traffic, which does not stop impersonation by already trusted devices; the RFC calls this an area for a future specification. For MPL, Layer 2 security SHOULD be used and the configuration of multicast addresses MUST be secure. The RFC also notes that it is not clear how homenets will be managed, while management is mandatory in building control.
sections.eli5: Doors are locked with a shared key, and a new gadget joins with help from one already trusted. If one gadget goes bad, everybody changes the lock.

sections.title: Why Plain RPL Falls Short
sections.content:
Appendix A lists shortcomings of plain RPL for home and building networks, which P2P-RPL is meant to counter. Because the DAG is a tree, traffic between nodes in different branches goes up toward the root and down again, in some unfortunate cases three hops up and three down. That concentrates traffic near the root and makes battery-powered senders stay awake longer. Also, Trickle can slow DIO/DAO updates to a few times an hour in a stable DAG, and RPL has no way to restore connectivity reactively. A light command sent in that window can fail.

Appendix B explains why multiple paths matter even over one hop. It reports measurements by [RTN2011]: eight nodes spread over 30 square meters, all in each other's clear region, still saw latencies longer than a second for periods of minutes, only on working days. Sending each message over both a direct one-hop path and a two-hop path via a random neighbor reduced the probability of delays above 100 ms significantly.
sections.eli5: Even friends standing close can sometimes not hear each other. So it helps to also pass a note through a second friend, just in case.
